newsitem.title: USA: NYC ranks 15th of major metro areas in jobs -- study.
newsitem.headline: NYC ranks 15th of major metro areas in jobs -- study.

text.p: New York City ranked 15th out of 20 major metropolitan areas when measured by employment growth, the city comptroller said Monday, though in 1996 it achieved the second biggest rise in employment since 1987.

The Olympic games and techology start-up companies propelled Atlanta to the top of the list with a 4.89 percent rate, followed by Seattle, which benefitted from hiring by key employers Microsoft and Boeing to achieve a 3.76 percent rate, according to a report based on the first 11 months of 1996 data by New York City Comptroller Alan Hevesi.

New York City's 0.80 percent rate outpaced Pittsburgh at 0.57 percent, Washington, D.C. at 0.57 percent, Newark at 0.54 percent, Balitmore at negative 0.55 percent, and Philadelphia at negative 0.78 percent.
And New York City had the highest unemployment rate of the 20 cities at 8.6 percent, more than double the rates of Washington, D.C., Boston, St Louis, San Francisco and Dallas.
In all of 1996, the city gained 37,100 private-sector jobs in 1996 for a 1.3 percent rate, the biggest rise in two years, though growth slowed significantly in the second half.

This was the second biggest increase since 1987, the last year of strong growth before a long local recession began, when private sector jobs expanded by 1.4 percent. This rate was slightly exceeded in 1994, when it hit 1.5 percent.

Still, the latest data show that the city's economy was slipping, as in the second half, the private sector only increased by 8,500 jobs, down sharply from the 28,300 added in the first half, according to Hevesi's report.

In December, employment fell by 2,000 jobs from the previous month, only the second time in five years that the number of jobs has fallen in this month. Most of the losses were seen in the private sector, which shed 1,700 jobs, with government losing 300 positions.
During 1996, total employment rose by 23,900 jobs, a 0.7 percent gain, as government jobs decreased by 13,200.

The financial sector shed 2,800 jobs while manufacturing lost 5,100 positions. Most of the growth was concentrated in services, which added 33,300 jobs, and wholesale and retail trade, which grew by 9,400 jobs.
